Amid the climate crisis and the 2060 Net Zero Emission target, the TikTok account @eos_indonesia plays a role as a communication actor actively promoting electric vehicles with a safe and comfortable narrative through digital content, in contrast to competitors who generally only focus on the technical aspects of the product. This study aims to identify how sustainability messages are constructed through visual elements, language, and narrative as a form of marketing in sustainability. This study uses a content analysis method, combining a sustainability communication approach and securitization theory. The focus of this research is on the framing strategies used by TikTok content creator @eos_indonesia in marketing electric vehicles on social media. This study uses a qualitative research method with a content analysis approach. To ensure the depth of this data, several methods are used to collect information. These methods consist of interviews, digital participatory observation and documentation. The data collection is an analysis of the TikTok account @eos_indonesia content data that will be taken with a period of January - June 2026 according to the classification that has been made, the data collected includes: video content (visual, audio and narrative). and content analysis has stages, starting from determining the unit of information, data sampling, recoding or recoding data (coding), grouping based on certain categories until finally interpreting the meaning contained in the message content. The results of this study, as presented on the TikTok account @eos_indonesia, describe electric vehicles as the newest and most environmentally friendly transportation solution, which is conveyed through educational content narratives and highlights the benefits of electric vehicles in everyday life. The published content consistently builds the view that the use of electric vehicles is safe, comfortable, and beneficial for environmental sustainability. This strengthens public acceptance of the transition to more sustainable transportation.

title: The ESG Banking Barometer
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: The ESG Banking Barometer is an annual, independent benchmark of ESG reporting across UK and Irish banks, building societies and fintechs, assessed entirely from public disclosures. The 2026 edition, its fourth, covers 60 firms across four
content: The ESG Banking Barometer is an annual, independent benchmark of ESG reporting across UK and Irish banks, building societies and fintechs, assessed entirely from public disclosures. The 2026 edition, its fourth, covers 60 firms across four sub-sectors and four ownership types, from annual reports and supplementary documents published on or before 30 June 2026. No survey responses, private disclosures or firm submissions are used, and no firm pays to be included. Headline findings. Forty of the 60 firms have set a net zero target and 19 have published a transition plan for reaching it, leaving 21 with a public pledge and no published route to it. Among the 17 firms reporting residential mortgage emissions intensity, disclosed figures range from 11.4 to 50.8 kgCO2e per square metre, a 4.5-fold difference across what is a comparatively homogeneous asset class; restating the two firms that use a loan-to-value weighted basis onto the PCAF basis narrows that to 2.8-fold. Aggregating the reported intensities by market share implies 88.3 MtCO2e from UK homes against 66.0 MtCO2e in the government's own statistics, an overstatement of 34%. Twenty-seven firms restated a prior year emissions figure, and 15 of the 60 obtain assurance over their greenhouse gas emissions, mostly at limited assurance level. Method. Each firm is assessed against 14 indicators spanning transition planning and materiality, GHG and financed emissions, climate targets, nature and carbon, and the structure of the reporting itself. Every figure is traceable to a named public document. Where a firm's disclosure is ambiguous the Barometer records it as unclear rather than inferring, and where two firms calculate the same metric on different bases the difference is reported rather than normalised away. Contents. This deposit contains the full report as PDF (14 indicators, 34 charts, the cohort list, a glossary and the method) and the public dataset as a workbook with three sheets: the firm-year Database, a Firms sheet giving each firm's sub-sector, ownership and size brackets, and a Field Dictionary defining every column. Firms are pseudonymised in the dataset, and the same identifier refers to the same firm in every Barometer year, so a firm can be followed across the four-year panel. Firm names are not published in the dataset; the report names the cohort.

title: A Rapid Chemical Relithiation Method Using Solvated Electrons for the Direct Recycling of Lithium-ion Battery Cathodes
summary: Due to the increasing adoption of electric vehicles, there is an imminent surge in waste lithium-ion batteries which will intensify resource depletion, environmental concerns, and supply chain vulnerability. Direct recycling is an energy-ef
content: Due to the increasing adoption of electric vehicles, there is an imminent surge in waste lithium-ion batteries which will intensify resource depletion, environmental concerns, and supply chain vulnerability. Direct recycling is an energy-efficient, environmentally friendly solution that nondestructively regenerates spent cathode active material, bypassing downstream cathode resynthesis from raw materials and securing critical minerals within the supply chain to meet growing battery demand while mitigating battery waste. Here we present a rapid solution-phase relithiation mechanism, inspired by Birch reduction chemistry, for the direct regeneration of spent LiNi0.5Mn0.3Co0.2O2 active material. Our method addresses limitations of direct recycling related to process intensity and scalability. A highly stable solvated electron solution, composed of pure Li metal and condensed liquid ammonia, efficiently delivers electrons to oxidized transition metals and supplies Li ions to vacancies within the crystal lattice, replenishing stoichiometric Li content. After a short annealing, the regenerated cathode material exhibits a restored bulk and near-surface crystal structure. The regenerated material demonstrates enhanced electrochemical performance relative to the pristine material when cycled to 4.3 V (159.49 mAh/g and 94.10% capacity retention after 100 cycles), highlighting its strong long-term cycling stability. Our system demonstrates the successful application of solvated electrons for efficient, sustainable battery recycling.

title: Visualizing the trends of green banking services and environmental performance
summary: Green services of banks go beyond corporate social responsibility initiatives; banks need to take a responsible role in supporting and financing environmentally friendly projects for a sustainable economy. This paper aims to identify trends
content: Green services of banks go beyond corporate social responsibility initiatives; banks need to take a responsible role in supporting and financing environmentally friendly projects for a sustainable economy. This paper aims to identify trends in green banking services and suggests implications and directions for future research. Using the Scopus database, science-mapping techniques applied to bibliometrics, along with data visualization tools such as VOS viewer and RStudio, were used to analyze citation, authorship, keyword co-occurrence, and collaboration networks among countries to identify the underlying clusters of green banking services. Then, 35 selected papers on green services of bank were reviewed using the theories, contexts, and methods (TCM) framework and the antecedents-decisions-outcomes (ADO) model. The study highlights the core theoretical constructs used by researchers. It categorizes green banking services antecedents into three groups: green operations, policy practices, and products & services, while highlighting the actionable environmental performance outcomes. This research will assist scholars, practitioners, and policymakers in gaining a clear understanding of green banking services dynamics and their environmental performance measures.

title: Climate Change Finance and Carbon Offsets: Addressing Global Climate Challenges through Innovative Funding and Emissions Reduction Mechanisms
source: Journal of the University of Ruhuna
summary: The global climate finance landscape remains insufficient to meet Paris Agreement targets, with unclear contributions from public, private, and voluntary carbon market flows. This study analyzed the structure and sufficiency of global clima
content: The global climate finance landscape remains insufficient to meet Paris Agreement targets, with unclear contributions from public, private, and voluntary carbon market flows. This study analyzed the structure and sufficiency of global climate finance flows against those targets using secondary quantitative data from key repositories (CPI, MDB Climate Finance Reports, BNEF, Ecosystem Marketplace), assessed for additionality, concessionally, and Paris alignment. Total tracked climate finance flows for 2019 were approximately 579 billion, comprising 253 billion from public sources and 326 billion from private investment in renewable energy. A detailed breakdown reveals foundational but insufficient public finance: Multi lateral Development Bank (MDB) climate finance total led 61.6 billion, with 67% directed to low- and middle-income countries. Private investment was concentrated in renewable energy, with combined global wind and solar investment reaching 269 billion in 2019. The analysis identifies the Voluntary Carbon Market (VCM) as a potential bridging mechanism, though one facing severe contraction and integrity challenges. Transaction volume exceeded 100 MtCO2e in 2020, dominated by forestry projects (52723 million, with a 56% year-on-year volume decline, signalling buyer hesitancy due to pervasive limitations. These include uncertainty regarding additionality, permanence risk, systemic over-crediting (with a significant share of credits failing new integrity benchmarks), and insufficient equity and data governance. The study concludes that while scaling proven mechanisms like green bonds is necessary, it is insufficient alone. Aligning financial flows with climate imperatives requires coupling this scale with rigorous reforms to carbon offset verification, strengthened market governance, and more transparent reporting to address critical integrity and data quality gaps.

title: ASSESSING THE SIGNIFICANCE OF PERFORMANCE INDICATORS (PIs) FOR GREEN PUBLIC PROCUREMENT (GPP) IMPLEMENTATION
source: International Journal of Built Environment and Earth Science
summary: Green Public Procurement (GPP) serves as a strategic policy instrument for leveraging state purchasing power to drive environmental sustainability, resource efficiency, and market transformation. However, evaluating the operational efficacy
content: Green Public Procurement (GPP) serves as a strategic policy instrument for leveraging state purchasing power to drive environmental sustainability, resource efficiency, and market transformation. However, evaluating the operational efficacy of GPP implementation across public sector organizations remains challenging due to fragmented performance measurement frameworks. This paper assesses the significance of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) in evaluating GPP implementation across public sector Ministries, Departments, and Agencies (MDAs). This paper specifically identifies, assesses, and determines the significance of PIs for GPP implementation within the Public Procuring Entities (PPEs). This study adopted both realist ontology stance and positivist epistemology perspective as its philosophical stance and employed a quantitative research design. A total of 254 questionnaires were distributed to respondents (i.e. procurement officers from the Federal Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs) in Nigeria). A total of 141 valid questionnaires were retrieved from the survey which represents 55.5% of valid response rate and subsequently analysed using descriptive statistics with the aid of Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) and python 3.14.3 amd64. Utilizing a quantitative research design, data were collected from procurement practitioners across MDAs and analyzed using descriptive statistical metrics, one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), and Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA). The study determined that the Nigerian MDAs possess exceptional internal consistency (alpha=0.963) demonstrating research instrument excellent reliability. The descriptive findings reveal that Policy Integration and Mandate into Regulatory Structures (Overall Mean=4.55, SD=0.78) and Monitoring and Evaluation of Resource and Energy Efficiency (Overall Mean=4.55, SD=0.71) emerged as joint top-ranked performance indicators (Rank=1). Conversely, socio-economic dimensions such as Gender Responsiveness in Public Procurement Distribution (Overall Mean=3.34, Rank=17) recorded lower relative prioritization. ANOVA results (F=2.338, p=0.07654) demonstrate no statistically significant divergence across institutional tiers (p>0.05), confirming a unified structural consensus on GPP performance metrics across MDAs. Furthermore, EFA extracted three latent dimensions accounting for 75.34% of cumulative variance: Environmental Accountability & Regulatory Mandates (42.87%), Operational Stakeholder Collaboration & Supply Chain Oversight (17.44%), and Socio-Economic Governance & Operational Equality Systems (15.03%). The study concludes that while public sector performance frameworks are heavily anchored in hard legal mandates and technical eco-efficiency metrics, achieving full green practice requires elevating supply-chain due diligence and socioeconomic equality criteria. Strategic recommendations are provided for policymakers, procuring entities, and supply chain partners.

title: Environmental industry-linked directors and firm green innovation: Evidence from China
summary: Using data on Chinese listed firms from 2016 to 2023, this study examines how environmental industry interlocking directors -- defined as directors who serve on the boards of firms in the environmental industry -- affect firms’ green innova
content: Using data on Chinese listed firms from 2016 to 2023, this study examines how environmental industry interlocking directors -- defined as directors who serve on the boards of firms in the environmental industry -- affect firms’ green innovation. We find that the presence of such directors significantly promotes firms’ green innovation. This effect is more pronounced in regions with weaker environmental regulatory stringency, in industries with more severe pollution, and among firms facing greater financing constraints. Mechanism analysis reveals that environmental industry interlocking directors facilitate green innovation through three channels: strengthening firms’ environmental orientation, attracting green investors, and improving firms’ access to environmental subsidies. Further analysis demonstrates that green innovation associated with these directors is associated with a high probability of obtaining environmental certifications and lower carbon emissions. Overall, this study reveals the role of interlocking directors in promoting firms’ green innovation and highlights the potential of sharing directors with environmental industry to advance environmental protection. These findings provide important implications for addressing major challenges in sustainable development.

title: AI-Enabled Decision Making and Competitive Advantage: A Knowledge-Based and Dynamic Capabilities Perspective
summary: This study examines how organizations create competitive advantage from AI-enabled decision-making capability by investigating the mediating roles of knowledge integration and dynamic capabilities within digital business ecosystems. Drawing
content: This study examines how organizations create competitive advantage from AI-enabled decision-making capability by investigating the mediating roles of knowledge integration and dynamic capabilities within digital business ecosystems. Drawing on the Knowledge-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the study explores the organizational mechanisms through which AI-enabled resources contribute to superior competitive outcomes. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 426 managers and professionals working in organizations that actively utilize artificial intelligence technologies across North America. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. Reliability, validity, mediation, and predictive assessments were performed using a bootstrapping procedure with 5,000 resamples. The results indicate that AI-enabled decision-making capability is positively associated with knowledge integration and dynamic capabilities. Knowledge integration positively influences dynamic capabilities and competitive advantage, while dynamic capabilities emerge as the strongest predictor of competitive advantage. The findings further reveal that knowledge integration mediates the relationship between AI-enabled decision-making capability and dynamic capabilities, while dynamic capabilities mediate the relationship between knowledge integration and competitive advantage. This study contributes to the artificial intelligence and digital business ecosystem literature by integrating the Knowledge-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities Theory within a single explanatory framework. The findings demonstrate that AI-driven competitive advantage emerges through knowledge integration and capability development rather than through technology adoption alone, providing new insights into how organizations can transform AI investments into sustainable strategic value.

title: Identifying optimal straw return strategies for crop production using meta‐analysis and interpretable machine learning
source: Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture
summary: Abstract BACKGROUND Straw return is widely promoted to improve soil fertility and crop productivity, but its climate consequences remain uncertain because yield gains may be accompanied by increased greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. A total o
content: Abstract BACKGROUND Straw return is widely promoted to improve soil fertility and crop productivity, but its climate consequences remain uncertain because yield gains may be accompanied by increased greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. A total of 5570 observations from published field studies were synthesized to quantify global responses of crop yield, N₂O, CO₂, CH₄, global warming potential (GWP), and greenhouse gas intensity (GHGI) to straw incorporation. Extreme Gradient Boosting, Shapley additive explanations, and bootstrap analysis were integrated to identify the dominant drivers and management thresholds for balancing productivity and climate impacts. RESULTS Straw return increased crop yield by 5.02%, but also increased N₂O emissions by 12.64%, CO₂ emissions by 31.39%, and CH₄ emissions by 34.85%, resulting in increases of 57.30% in GWP and 80.94% in GHGI. These responses were strongly regulated by crop type, straw‐return rate, incorporation depth, return duration, fertilization, and climatic conditions. Straw‐return rate was the dominant predictor of N 2 O emissions, whereas mean annual precipitation was the primary predictor of CO 2 and CH 4 emissions. Management practices involving a straw‐return rate of approximately 5 t ha⁻¹, a return duration of 1–3 years, and the use of maize or wheat straw rather than rice straw were associated with a more favorable balance between crop yield and GHG emissions. Estimated agronomic thresholds for fertilization were 180 kg N ha −1 , 75 kg P 2 O 5 ha −1 , and 180 kg K 2 O ha −1 , whereas environmental thresholds for limiting GWP and GHGI were 210 kg N ha −1 , 40–100 kg P 2 O 5 ha −1 , and 100 kg K 2 O ha −1 . CONCLUSION These findings demonstrate that straw return is not universally beneficial for the climate but can be optimized through crop‐specific and climate‐adapted residue and nutrient management. The study provides global quantitative evidence for designing climate‐smart straw‐return strategies that reconcile food production with GHG mitigation across agroecosystems. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

title: A dynamic recommendation algorithm for regional industry-adapted higher vocational courses integrating counterfactual causal inference and graph neural networks
summary: The mismatch between higher vocational curricula and the shifting skill demands of regional industries continues to constrain graduate employability, while existing recommendation engines remain trapped in correlational logic and selection-
content: The mismatch between higher vocational curricula and the shifting skill demands of regional industries continues to constrain graduate employability, while existing recommendation engines remain trapped in correlational logic and selection-biased enrollment histories. This paper proposes CCIG-DRec, a dynamic course recommendation algorithm that couples heterogeneous graph neural networks with counterfactual causal inference. A time-evolving graph linking students, courses, occupational posts, skills, and industries is constructed from recruitment portals and open vocational catalogs across the Chengdu–Chongqing Economic Circle, and sliding-window snapshots are refreshed through relation-specific exponential decay whose half-lives are estimated from observed edge-persistence curves rather than assumed. A dual attention scheme operating at node and meta-path levels produces type-aware embeddings, after which a causal intervention layer reweights neighbor messages by clipped, self-normalized exposure propensities to neutralize industry popularity bias. Counterfactual student trajectories generated through abduction–action–prediction supply both training signals and interventional explanations for each recommended course. Against the strongest of five competitive baselines, each granted the same five-type graph and the same industry signal, CCIG-DRec raises Recall@10 by 12.7 percent and NDCG@10 by 11.8 percent on the regional corpus and narrows the counterfactual fairness gap by 30.4 percent, every margin significant at $$p$$ < 0.01 under a paired test over ten seeds. The industry adaptation margin behaves differently, and the paper says so plainly: it shrinks from 13.0 to 4.6 percent once every baseline receives an equivalent industry-fit regularizer, while a placement-based indicator that enters no training objective puts the surviving advantage at 5.1 percent. Results on the public MOOCCube benchmark are reported alongside the regional corpus. Cross-scenario tests across five industrial clusters confirm stable performance under varying demand structures, and a case study demonstrates auditable interventional justifications suitable for program-level curricular governance.

title: Identifying the influencing factors of lake surface greenhouse gas concentrations using sentinel-2 remote sensing and machine learning: A case study of bird Island, Qinghai Lake
summary: Alpine lakes on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau are important regions for studies of the regional carbon cycle and are highly sensitive to climate change. However, the variation patterns of lake surface greenhouse gases and their environmental re
content: Alpine lakes on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau are important regions for studies of the regional carbon cycle and are highly sensitive to climate change. However, the variation patterns of lake surface greenhouse gases and their environmental regulation mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, Bird Island of Qinghai Lake was selected as the study area. Based on the measured concentrations of lake surface CO 2 , CH 4 , and H 2 O corresponding to Sentinel-2 satellite overpass periods throughout 2021, combined with Sentinel-2 remote sensing imagery and ERA5-Land meteorological data, Random Forest (RF) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) models, together with the SHAP method, were used to identify and predict the influencing factors and their contribution characteristics to the variations in lake surface CO 2 , CH 4 , and H 2 O. The results showed that CO 2 , CH 4 , and H 2 O exhibited distinct seasonal variations. The annual variation in CO 2 concentration generally showed a “V”-shaped pattern, with concentrations during the growing season being lower than those during the non-growing season. The annual variation in CH 4 concentration was relatively small and exhibited a “wave”-shaped pattern. The H 2 O concentration showed a distinct unimodal pattern, and its high-value period was generally consistent with the low-value period of CO 2 . Temperature and MNDWI were the main predictive factors affecting the variations in CO 2 , CH 4 , and H 2 O concentrations, while H 2 O concentration was also affected by Radiation. This study combined observational data, remote sensing imagery, and machine learning, providing new insights into the environmental predictive factors of greenhouse gas concentrations in lakes under climate change.

title: Building For Heat
summary: Building For Heat examines how vernacular buildings and settlements moderate heat, and how their environmental principles can inform contemporary design in arid regions. It connects climatic exposure, building physics, patterns of occupatio
content: Building For Heat examines how vernacular buildings and settlements moderate heat, and how their environmental principles can inform contemporary design in arid regions. It connects climatic exposure, building physics, patterns of occupation, and access to cooling, with attention to the conditions under which inherited approaches remain useful. Across five chapters, the book explores shade, courtyards, windcatchers, ventilation, thermal mass, and evaporative cooling; considers ways to evaluate indoor comfort and neighbourhood microclimates; and examines the consequences of standardized construction and dependence on mechanical cooling. It then brings these themes into design, retrofit, and policy discussions for arid environments. Written for architects, architectural engineers, researchers, students, and practitioners, the book presents the Vernacular Cooling Performance Framework and Passive Cooling Gap Index as proposed tools for organizing evidence and assessment. It emphasizes local validation, climate limits, maintenance, water availability, air quality, and occupant needs when translating vernacular knowledge into climate-adaptive practice.

title: Micro-processes of paradoxical learning: how entrepreneurs reconcile financial and ESG tensions
summary: This study explores the micro-processes through which entrepreneurs learn to reconcile the inherent paradoxical tensions between financial viability and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) goals. Drawing on organizational paradox th
content: This study explores the micro-processes through which entrepreneurs learn to reconcile the inherent paradoxical tensions between financial viability and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) goals. Drawing on organizational paradox theory and entrepreneurial learning, we conducted in-depth interviews with entrepreneurs leading ventures that explicitly integrate financial and ESG objectives. Relying on a Gioia methodology for inductive analysis, we developed a process model of paradoxical learning that reveals four interconnected micro-processes: (1) cognitive reframing, (2) emotional regulation, (3) behavioral experimentation, and (4) social sensemaking. Our findings demonstrate that entrepreneurs move through three distinct phases of paradoxical learning: (a) tension recognition, (b) paradox acceptance, and (c) integration capability development. We find that digital technologies, digital business models, and digitally mediated feedback loops shape these learning processes in distinctive ways, accelerating experimentation cycles, enabling distributed sensemaking across digital ecosystems, and providing data-driven tools for developing integration capabilities. The findings contribute to entrepreneurial learning theory by revealing the dynamic capabilities required for managing persistent contradictions, extending organizational paradox theory to the entrepreneurial context, and offering practical insights for entrepreneurs seeking to foster integrated value creation. The study reveals that successful ESG integration requires not just strategic thinking but fundamental shifts in how entrepreneurs perceive, experience, and resolve competing demands, with digital ventures facing unique tensions and opportunities that shape the nature and trajectory of paradoxical learning.

title: Knowledge Access in Kenya’s Clean Energy Entrepreneurship: Understanding Ecosystem Constraints for Women and Youth
summary: Clean energy transitions are increasingly recognized as central to addressing climate change and expanding economic opportunities, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. However, participation in clean energy entrepreneurship is
content: Clean energy transitions are increasingly recognized as central to addressing climate change and expanding economic opportunities, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. However, participation in clean energy entrepreneurship is shaped not only by access to finance and technology, but also by access to knowledge. This study examines how knowledge access influences women- and youth-led clean energy enterprises in Kenya. Using a cross-sectional mixed-methods approach, the study draws on survey data from 891 enterprises and qualitative insights from key informant interviews. The findings show that most entrepreneurs experience significant constraints in accessing knowledge related to business development, regulatory processes, and growth strategies. While descriptive analysis suggests variation across education levels, regression results identify sector participation as the most consistent predictor of knowledge access. The findings provide evidence for policymakers and ecosystem actors to strengthen inclusive knowledge-sharing systems, improve coordination among support institutions, and design targeted interventions that enhance the growth of women- and youth-led clean energy enterprises while accelerating Kenya's clean energy transition.

title: Biosensors for Food Safety and Adulteration Monitoring: Applications, Smart Packaging Integration, and Pathways to Intelligent, Field‐Deployable Detection Systems
summary: ABSTRACT Food safety and authenticity remain major global public health concerns, necessitating rapid, sensitive, and cost‐effective analytical tools. This review critically evaluates recent advances in biosensing technologies for food safe
content: ABSTRACT Food safety and authenticity remain major global public health concerns, necessitating rapid, sensitive, and cost‐effective analytical tools. This review critically evaluates recent advances in biosensing technologies for food safety monitoring, food adulteration detection, smart packaging, and data‐driven digital biosensing, providing an integrated perspective beyond the scope of previous reviews. Electrochemical, optical, and piezoelectric biosensors demonstrate remarkable analytical performance, enabling sub‐CFU pathogen detection and ppb‐level quantification of chemical contaminants across diverse food matrices, including milk, meat, seafood, cereals, and edible oils. Integration with smart packaging, such as colorimetric freshness indicators, pH‐responsive films, and on‐package contamination sensors, enables real‐time, non‐destructive quality assessment without conventional laboratory infrastructure. Furthermore, the convergence of biosensors with the Internet of Things (IoT), smartphone‐based imaging, machine learning, and cloud computing has accelerated the development of intelligent, connected food safety monitoring systems. Despite these advances, challenges related to matrix effects, long‐term stability, scalability, commercialization, standardization, and regulatory approval continue to hinder widespread implementation. This review critically discusses these limitations while highlighting commercialization strategies, technology readiness, and future research directions, including microfluidic integration, biodegradable sensing materials, explainable artificial intelligence, and blockchain‐enabled traceability, to support the development of reliable, scalable, and globally deployable food safety monitoring systems.

title: DESIGNING GREEN BONDS FOR RENEWABLE ENERGY SMEs IN SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA
source: International Journal of Built Environment and Earth Science
summary: Over 90% of sub-Saharan African (SSA) businesses are SMEs and key drivers of renewable energy diffusion, yet limited climate finance, driven by high perceived risk, weak credit histories, and underdeveloped capital markets, constrains their
content: Over 90% of sub-Saharan African (SSA) businesses are SMEs and key drivers of renewable energy diffusion, yet limited climate finance, driven by high perceived risk, weak credit histories, and underdeveloped capital markets, constrains their investment capacity. Green bonds have mobilised institutional capital for low-carbon transitions in OECD markets, but their design misaligns with SSA's renewable energy SME sector, where currency mismatches, aggregation failures, and inadequate de-risking create structural barriers. This study develops a green bond design methodology for SSA's renewable energy SMEs using a mixed-methods approach: financial instrument analysis; synthesis of secondary data from six countries (Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, South Africa, Rwanda, Senegal); a systematic review of issuance reports and investor disclosures; and a financial modelling system that simulates bond performance under risk-sharing, currency-hedging, and blended finance structures. The paper contributes architectural innovations (local-currency tranches, aggregation platforms, first-loss reserves, results-based coupons), empirical evidence, and policy recommendations for regional standards and sovereign credit enhancement, advancing the adaptation of green finance to emerging-economy contexts.

title: Bacteriological Assessment of Escherichia coli and Salmonella spp. from Local Meat Shops in Dhaka, Bangladesh
source: International journal of medical and health research.
summary: Retail meat and contact surfaces of meat have been identified as reservoirs of foodborne pathogens and can be used to transmit antimicrobial-resistant bacteria to consumers. In this research, the prevalence, phenotypic identification, molec
content: Retail meat and contact surfaces of meat have been identified as reservoirs of foodborne pathogens and can be used to transmit antimicrobial-resistant bacteria to consumers. In this research, the prevalence, phenotypic identification, molecular confirmation, antimicrobial resistance, and biofilm-forming capability of Escherichia coli and Salmonella spp. were determined in local meat shop in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Twelve samples (raw meat portions and environmental swabs) were sampled, 8 of which were subjected to microbiological analysis. Presumptive isolates were subcultured on MacConkey (MAC) and Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate (XLD) agar and identified by Triple Sugar Iron (TSI), citrate utilization and Motility-Indole-Urease (MIU) assays. The biochemical characteristics of most XLD-derived isolates were similar to Salmonella spp. and the majority of MAC-derived isolates were similar to E. coli. Molecular verification was added with the help of Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on the invA gene of Salmonella spp. and the uidA gene of E. coli. The Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion method of antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed widespread resistance, with about 70% of the tested isolates having a multidrug-resistant phenotype and no isolates being completely susceptible to all antibiotics tested. Biofilm formation, as measured using the microtiter plate assay, revealed that all the isolates tested were biofilm formers with optical densities of 0.105 to 0.35. It was also found that stronger biofilm formation was mostly seen in XLD-derived isolates compared to MAC-derived isolates. The results indicate an important food safety issue and the necessity of heightened hygiene, regular monitoring, and sensible antimicrobial usage.

title: Iranian farmers’ pro-environmental behaviors supporting human wetland coexistence
summary: The application of pro-environmental behaviors in wetlands—particularly sensitive and valuable ecosystems such as Zaribar—is critically important, as these areas play a vital role in both biodiversity conservation and the livelihoods of loc
content: The application of pro-environmental behaviors in wetlands—particularly sensitive and valuable ecosystems such as Zaribar—is critically important, as these areas play a vital role in both biodiversity conservation and the livelihoods of local communities. When individuals and local communities adopt sustainable and environmentally friendly practices, the gradual degradation of wetlands can be prevented, creating conditions in which human and ecological needs are met simultaneously. This study was conducted with the overarching aim of identifying the factors influencing farmers’ adoption of pro-environmental behaviors in wetlands. The statistical population consisted of all farmers in the Zaribar wetland area of Kurdistan Province in western Iran. The extended theory of planned behavior (TPB) was employed as the theoretical framework, incorporating two additional variables: environmental concern (EC) and environmental knowledge (EK). The results revealed that the extended TPB model improved the explanatory power of the initial model by 20.3% in predicting farmers’ pro-environmental behaviors in wetlands. In other words, attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioral control, environmental concern, and environmental knowledge all had positive and significant effects. Overall, the findings suggest that integrating psychological, social, and perceptual factors provides a valuable framework for policymakers in wetland management and sustainable agriculture.

title: Data-driven real estate valuation, part II: data, uncertainty and governance for reliable automated valuation models in practice
source: Journal of Property Investment and Finance
summary: Purpose This paper is part II of a two-part review of automated valuation models (AVMs). Part II examines what is required for AVMs to be reliable, fair and production-ready in high-stakes valuation practice, focussing on validation, uncert
content: Purpose This paper is part II of a two-part review of automated valuation models (AVMs). Part II examines what is required for AVMs to be reliable, fair and production-ready in high-stakes valuation practice, focussing on validation, uncertainty quantification, market coverage, data enrichment including environmental, social and governance (ESG) and synthetic data, fairness and bias, and governance. Part I covers the methodological foundations, the AVM pipeline and the main model families. Design/methodology/approach The paper follows the same narrative, practitioner informed review approach set out in Part I, synthesising peer-reviewed literature, binding regulatory and professional standards, and publicly available AVM provider documentation. Findings are consolidated in an evidence map that distinguishes established, emerging and speculative claims. Findings The review identifies four findings. First, data quality and granularity set the upper bound of AVM performance more fundamentally than model complexity. Second, calibrated prediction intervals and periodic backtesting are prerequisites for high-stakes use. Third, ESG signals and synthetic data expand the AVM data frontier but remain governance-sensitive. Fourth, hybrid human and AVM architectures prove most resilient, aligning with empirical and regulatory expectations. Practical implications Providers should attach calibrated prediction intervals to every AVM output. Users should monitor performance through periodic backtesting and bias audits. Regulators should treat AVM governance as part of broader model risk management. Originality/value The paper offers an integrative synthesis of data, uncertainty and governance in AVMs and positions hybrid human and AVM architectures as the most defensible operating model under current regulatory expectations.

title: Estimated enteric methane emissions and performance of crossbred dairy cows in two location-based feeding systems in northern Ethiopia
summary: This observational survey-based study provided a descriptive comparison of methane (CH 4 ) emissions and performance of crossbred dairy cows across two location-based feeding systems in northern Ethiopia. Input and output data were collecte
content: This observational survey-based study provided a descriptive comparison of methane (CH 4 ) emissions and performance of crossbred dairy cows across two location-based feeding systems in northern Ethiopia. Input and output data were collected from 24 dairy farms through a combination of questionnaire survey and direct on-farm measurements. CH 4 emissions were estimated via Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Tier 2 procedures. The findings revealed that cows in Agula had numerically shorter age at first service (AFS; mean ± standard deviation (SD); 13.92 ± 0.83 months) and calving intervals (CI 13.75 ± 0.50 months) than those in Wukro (14.63 ± 0.29 and 14.38 ± 0.48 months, respectively). The average daily milk yield (ADMY) was numerically higher for cows in Agula (13.88 ± 2.85 L, L) than those in Wukro (12.79 ± 2.21 L). Major challenges in milk production in the study area included limited space, feed shortages and high feed costs. The estimated CH 4 emissions per mature, crossbred dairy cow were numerically higher in Agula (100 kg CH 4 head −1 yr −1 ) than those estimated for Wukro cows (88 kg CH 4 head −1 yr −1 ). However, on a per-kg-milk basis, the two location-based feeding systems were comparable in estimated CH 4 intensity, while the feeding system in Agula was associated with numerically higher milk yield and shorter AFS/CI.

title: Algorithmic urbanism and structural inequality: a critical assessment of artificial intelligence in urban systems
summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed to optimise urban energy systems, transport networks, and housing markets. However, its infrastructure frequently reproduces structural inequalities, imposing environmental and social costs o
content: Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed to optimise urban energy systems, transport networks, and housing markets. However, its infrastructure frequently reproduces structural inequalities, imposing environmental and social costs onto marginalised communities whilst concentrating benefits among capital-holding actors. This paper argues hypothesis that AI urbanism, as currently embedded within existing urban political economies, functions as a mechanism of cost externalisation rather than public service optimisation: efficiency gains accrue to capital-holding actors whilst costs are displaced onto marginalised communities and peripheral territories. This study adopts a qualitative, critical analytical approach, combi­ning a systematic literature synthesis with comparative case studies across three urban domains of energy, transport, and housing, drawing on evidence from both the Global North and the Global South. The informational basis combines peer-reviewed scholarship, intergo­vernmental reports, and investigative journalism. The study relies on secondary sources, which constitutes its principal limitation alongside the rapidly evolving nature of AI governance. The analysis revealed that AI data centre infrastruc­ture in Mesa, Arizona, extracted 5.5 million cubic metres of water annually whilst residential construction permits were simultaneously revo­ked due to aquifer depletion. In Caucaia, Brazil, a proposed data centre would consume electricity equivalent to 2.2 million households, exempli­fying computational colonialism in peripheral economies. In transport, the Waze for Cities programme in Joinville, Brazil, created extractive data dependency that undermined municipal governance capacity, whilst Singaporeʼs publicly governed system demonstrated that equitable outcomes are achievable under different gover­nance architectures. In housing, Barcelonaʼs Sant Marti district experienced algorithmic amplifi­cation of gentrification, displacing low-income residents despite environmental improvements. The paradox of AI urbanism is sustained not by technical failure but by the political economy in which these systems operate. The study provides recommendations for municipal authorities to implement public data trusts, participatory governance mechanisms, and wellbeing-oriented optimisation metrics, ensuring that AI-driven urban systems serve collective wellbeing over capital accumulation

title: Game complexity of pricing and emission reduction in low-carbon supply chains with government regulation and fairness concerns under stagflation risk
summary: Abstract Global climate and economic pressures necessitate low-carbon supply chain transitions, a process especially challenging for emerging markets and developing economies amid declining foreign investment and rising stagflation risks. T
content: Abstract Global climate and economic pressures necessitate low-carbon supply chain transitions, a process especially challenging for emerging markets and developing economies amid declining foreign investment and rising stagflation risks. This study uniquely integrates fairness concerns and stagflation risk into a nonlinear dynamical system, investigating a low-carbon supply chain consisting of a manufacturer and a capital-constrained retailer with fairness concerns. A dynamic Stackelberg game model is developed, incorporating government regulation on financing interest rates and fairness concerns. The principal findings are threefold. First, short-term analysis demonstrates the potential efficacy of government regulation within our model framework, showing that calibrated interventions via the financing rate ( $$\delta $$ ) and fairness concern adjustment coefficient (γ) can effectively guide the system toward a stable equilibrium under the specified parameter ranges. Second, long-term evolution reveals inherent instability: bounded rational strategy adjustments cause the system to cascade from period-doubling bifurcation into chaos once price adjustment speeds $$({v}_{1}, {v}_{2}$$ ) exceed critical thresholds (e.g., $${v}_{1}>0.239, {v}_{2}>0.3098$$ ), leading to severe performance deterioration. Third, the application of a time-delayed feedback control method shows promise in suppressing chaotic dynamics and restoring local stability within the simulated scenarios. These findings offer a novel theoretical lens for understanding supply chain instability and provide actionable insights for designing robust regulatory frameworks in volatile macroeconomic environments. Policymakers should manage price adjustment speeds and leverage synergistic carbon pricing and fairness regulations to mitigate instability and foster sustainable supply chain development.

title: An econometric analysis of the Greek wine industry’s performance determinants
source: International Journal of Wine Business Research
summary: Purpose This study aims to investigate the key determinants of firm performance in the Greek wine sector. The analysis focuses on firms’ balance sheet structure and operational characteristics, emphasizing liquidity conditions, debt composi
content: Purpose This study aims to investigate the key determinants of firm performance in the Greek wine sector. The analysis focuses on firms’ balance sheet structure and operational characteristics, emphasizing liquidity conditions, debt composition, working capital management, investment activity and firm-specific attributes. Design/methodology/approach This study uses panel data from 67 Greek wineries (2013–2024) to analyze profitability via return on assets. The model incorporates internal determinants, including liquidity, debt structure (short/long-term), working capital, capital expenditure, size and age, applying a one-year lag to financing and investment variables to account for delayed impacts. Estimation is performed using pooled ordinary least squares and random effects models, supported by diagnostic tests to ensure robustness. Findings The analysis reveals that liquidity, debt (short- and long-term), efficient working capital management and investment activity all significantly boost firm performance. Notably, long-term debt shows a stronger positive impact on ROA than short-term debt, emphasizing the importance of strategic financing for long-term growth. Conversely, firm size is negatively correlated with performance, pointing toward diseconomies of scale or increased coordination costs in large operations. Profitability is driven primarily by financial metrics rather than the length of time a firm has been operating. Originality/value This research contributes to the literature on the Greek wine industry, presents empirical data on the factors that shape business performance and supports the design of effective strategies and policies.

title: ECONOMICS OF ECOSYSTEM SERVICES FROM AGRICULTURAL WASTE RECYCLING SYSTEM: CASE STUDY OF THE FEDERAL CAPITAL TERRITORY
source: International Journal of African Sustainable Development Research
summary: Agriculture in Nigeria is multi-dimensional, producing food, feed, fibre, and fuel, while also providing intangible ecosystem services that largely remain un-priced. Because farmers are not compensated for these services, the adoption of ec
content: Agriculture in Nigeria is multi-dimensional, producing food, feed, fibre, and fuel, while also providing intangible ecosystem services that largely remain un-priced. Because farmers are not compensated for these services, the adoption of eco-friendly technologies for sustainable agricultural development is constrained. Concurrently, the conversion of agricultural residues into value-added products has emerged as a strategic pathway for economic transformation and circularity. This study investigated the economics of ecosystem services from agricultural waste recycling systems and their effect on smallholder welfare in Nigeria, with a case study of the Federal Capital Territory [FCT]. Agricultural residues, often treated as environmental liabilities, possess significant economic potential when processed into products such as biogas, organic fertilizer, bio-briquettes, and biochar. Using secondary data from 2015 to 2024, and FCT-specific data for the 2022/2023 production cycle, the study: Identified and quantified waste streams; estimated the economic value of provisioning and regulating ecosystem services; assessed contributions to smallholder income and rural employment; evaluated the level of adoption of eco-friendly recycling technologies; and lastly, examined policy factors influencing monetization. Findings for FCT show an annual generation of 547,199 tonnes of bio-waste, with potential to produce 17.39 million m³ of biogas and 98,943 tonnes of biochar. The economic potential was estimated at ₦17.45 billion per year. Environmentally, utilization can avoid 369,095 tonnes of CO2e per year. The findings provide empirical evidence to address the data gap in the National Climate Change Policy for Nigeria 2021–2030 and support integration of agro-waste recycling into Nigeria’s circular bio-economy.

title: “Cannabis Green Wave” versus “Nicotine Freeze”: the regulatory paradox of cannabis liberalization and nicotine prohibition
summary: BACKGROUND: The contemporary landscape of psychoactive substance regulation is characterized by a striking policy paradox. On one hand there is the gradual liberalization and mainstreaming of the cannabis market (the "Green Wave"), propelle
content: BACKGROUND: The contemporary landscape of psychoactive substance regulation is characterized by a striking policy paradox. On one hand there is the gradual liberalization and mainstreaming of the cannabis market (the "Green Wave"), propelled by principles such as human rights, harm reduction, criminal justice reform, social equity, and economic efficiency. This coincides with a neo-prohibitionist tightening of regulations against non-combustible, harm reduction nicotine products (the "Nicotine Freeze"). This manuscript interrogates the toxicological, sociological, and bioethical inconsistencies driving this divergence. ANALYSIS: Decoupling the active compounds (THC and nicotine) from their traditional combustible delivery systems reveals a stark regulatory asymmetry. Toxicologically, while the primary harms of both substances appear to stem from combustion, state policies heavily restrict lower-risk, non-combustible nicotine alternatives while facilitating access to smokeable and edible cannabis. Neurocognitively, nicotine functions as a non-intoxicating stimulant with potential cognitive benefits, whereas cannabis, particularly sustained and heavy use, carries risks of cognitive impairment and psychosis. Furthermore, a glaring double standard exists regarding youth protection: the "gateway theory" and flavor bans are aggressively weaponized to prohibit nicotine alternatives, while cannabis products become progressively more palatable and include potentially youth-appealing flavored products with minimal precautionary resistance. Therefore, from a toxicological and public health perspective, these regulatory double standards indicate that the current treatment of nicotine versus cannabis repeats historical prohibition paradigms, which, despite toxicological arguments, were driven primarily by political ideology and prejudice rather than objective evidence. Sociologically, the strict prohibition of nicotine products ignores the "Iron Law of Prohibition," inadvertently fostering unregulated black markets-a historical lesson policymakers readily accept regarding cannabis. Bioethically, cannabis legalization is championed under the banner of "cognitive liberty" and adult autonomy, whereas nicotine regulation has regressed into "hard paternalism," infantilizing consumers and denying smokers' access to life-saving substitutes. CONCLUSION: Current regulatory frameworks are no longer neutral; they enforce a moral hierarchy that protects the pursuit of cannabis while punishing the management of functional nicotine dependence. The foundational arguments that characterize the current trend of cannabis legalization are systematically ignored in the case of harm reduction nicotine products. To optimize public health outcomes, regulators must resolve this paradox by abandoning selective paternalism and applying a consistent, risk-proportionate harm-reduction paradigm to all psychoactive substances.

title: Benzene diamine-crosslinked PVC/polycarbonate nanofiltration membranes with enhanced antifouling performance for emerging contaminant removal and water purification
summary: The crosslinking of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) with polycarbonate (PC) polymers was successfully achieved through a two-step reaction involving the attachment of benzene diamine to polyvinyl chloride, followed by linkage with polycarbonate. T
content: The crosslinking of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) with polycarbonate (PC) polymers was successfully achieved through a two-step reaction involving the attachment of benzene diamine to polyvinyl chloride, followed by linkage with polycarbonate. The resulting polymer was characterized using Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM). FT-IR analysis confirmed the presence of characteristic functional groups, indicating successful crosslinking. TGA and DSC analyses demonstrated enhanced thermal stability, with degradation occurring at elevated temperatures. The crosslinked PVC-PC polymer was then electrospun into nanofibrous membranes, which exhibited high water flux, excellent anti-fouling properties, and efficient salt rejection. The membranes also demonstrated significant removal of heavy metals and pharmaceutical contaminants from water, highlighting their potential in water purification applications. These findings suggest that the crosslinked PVC-PC polymer is a promising material for advanced membrane-based filtration technologies.

title: Upcycling carbon dioxide into precursors for pharmaceutical and agrochemical applications
summary: The rising concentration of greenhouse gases poses a serious threat to the global climate and ecosystems. Addressing these challenges requires effective carbon capture, utilization, and storage technologies. Among these, carbon dioxide util
content: The rising concentration of greenhouse gases poses a serious threat to the global climate and ecosystems. Addressing these challenges requires effective carbon capture, utilization, and storage technologies. Among these, carbon dioxide utilization (CDU) is one of the most promising approaches, as it supports a circular economy by converting waste carbon dioxide (CO₂) into value-added chemical precursors (VACPs). Existing reviews on CO₂ utilization have largely focused on fuels, bulk commodity chemicals, and polymer feedstocks, with limited attention given to VACPs for pharmaceutical and agrochemical applications, particularly heterocyclic and nitrogen-containing scaffolds. To address this gap, this review examines CO₂-derived VACPs for pharmaceutical and agrochemical applications. The review also provides an overview of recent advances in CDU technologies that enable the production of CO₂-derived VACPs. It explores the role of artificial intelligence in catalyst discovery, process optimization, and scale-up, and evaluates the feasibility, sustainability, and carbon footprint reduction potential of CO₂-derived manufacturing routes. By highlighting the potential of CO₂-derived precursor classes for pharmaceutical and agrochemical applications and reviewing recent advances in enabling technologies, this review provides a foundation for future research and the sustainable development of CO₂-derived manufacturing routes. Graphical Abstract

title: Compaction, CBR, and microstructural performance of lateritic soil stabilized with recycled concrete aggregate
summary: The continued reliance on energy-intensive hydraulic binders for soil stabilization presents a significant environmental challenge, prompting the need for sustainable, low-carbon alternatives. This study investigates the technical, microstr
content: The continued reliance on energy-intensive hydraulic binders for soil stabilization presents a significant environmental challenge, prompting the need for sustainable, low-carbon alternatives. This study investigates the technical, microstructural, and environmental performance of Recycled Concrete Aggregate (RCA) as a stabilizer for brown lateritic soil. A multi-scale experimental program was conducted, integrating microstructural characterization (X-ray Diffraction [XRD] and Scanning Electron Microscopy [SEM]) with macroscopic geotechnical evaluations (compaction and California Bearing Ratio [CBR]) at RCA replacement levels of 0–25%. Mineralogical analysis revealed the laterite to be a quartz-dominant ferruginous soil, while the RCA introduced calcium-rich anorthite and fibrous anthophyllite phases. SEM imaging showed that RCA addition promoted a rigid granular skeleton with mechanical interlocking and partial void infilling by fine particles. Geotechnical testing indicated that soil performance peaked at 20% RCA replacement, where Maximum Dry Density increased from 1.98 to 2.11 g/cm³, Optimum Moisture Content decreased from 9.5% to 8.0%, and soaked CBR improved from 30% to 41%. Replacements exceeding 20% led to performance declines attributed to matrix disruption and high-water absorption of the residual mortar. Environmental and cost analyses suggested that the optimized 20% RCA mixture can achieve a substantial reduction in CO₂ emissions (approximately 93%) compared to traditional 5% cement stabilization within the system boundary considered in this study. These findings indicate that RCA offers a promising circular-economy approach for improving the short-term mechanical properties of this lateritic soil, contributing to more sustainable road infrastructure development.

title: Raw meat based diets for dogs and their nutritional and One Health implications
summary: Raw meat-based diets (RMBDs) for dogs comprise heterogeneous commercial and home-prepared products that differ in formulation, processing, storage, and quality control. This critical narrative review evaluates RMBDs within a One Health fram
content: Raw meat-based diets (RMBDs) for dogs comprise heterogeneous commercial and home-prepared products that differ in formulation, processing, storage, and quality control. This critical narrative review evaluates RMBDs within a One Health framework, integrating evidence on nutritional adequacy, biological effects, microbiological hazards, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), zoonotic transmission, and environmental sustainability. Literature was identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and CAB Abstracts from January 2000 through August 2026, supplemented by reference-list and regulatory searches; evidence was weighted qualitatively according to study design, directness, sample size, analytical validity, control of alternative explanations, and consistency. Analytical studies show product-specific nutrient deviations in both commercial and home-prepared diets, but these findings should not be generalized to all RMBDs. Short-term studies often report high apparent total-tract digestibility and diet-associated changes in faecal microbiota and metabolites; however, comparisons frequently differ in ingredients, moisture, fibre, starch, fat, and energy density, limiting attribution to raw processing itself, and long-term clinical superiority has not been demonstrated. Contamination of raw pet food with Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes, and antimicrobial-resistant Enterobacterales is repeatedly documented. Raw feeding has also been repeatedly associated with increased faecal carriage of resistant E. coli in observational studies, although residual confounding remains possible. Environmental evidence is less mature and largely derives from pet foods generally: impacts are driven principally by the type and quantity of animal-derived ingredients, whereas additional effects of freezing, freeze-drying, transport, and storage are product- and system-dependent. Overall, RMBDs warrant product-specific and household-specific risk assessment rather than categorical judgement. Veterinary counselling should emphasize nutritionally complete formulation, transparent quality assurance, pathogen-reduction processes that reduce but do not eliminate microbiological risk, and strict hygiene while acknowledging uncertainty in long-term comparative outcomes.

title: The impact of sectoral policies and policy mixes on low-carbon innovation ‘take-offs’: an analysis of 18 countries 2001–2022
summary: Climate policy is a critical driver of low-carbon technology (LCT) innovation; however, prior studies pay insufficient attention to the combined effects of multiple policies. Addressing this deficiency, we combine machine learning with caus
content: Climate policy is a critical driver of low-carbon technology (LCT) innovation; however, prior studies pay insufficient attention to the combined effects of multiple policies. Addressing this deficiency, we combine machine learning with causal inference to endogenously detect sector-specific LCT ‘takeoffs’ in 18 major LCT nations from 2001–2022, systematically evaluating the impacts of over 1,600 policy interventions. Results show that some climate policy interventions act as key triggers for takeoffs in LCT innovation, with synergistic policy mixes forming the primary impact mechanism. In aggregate, market-based instruments (MBI), especially subsidies, serve as the foundational lever for innovation; non-market-based instruments (NMBI), notably performance standards, provide essential complementarity; and targets & governance (T&G) enhance long-run credibility and implementation capacity. At the sectoral level, the buildings sector exhibits the highest responsiveness to policy; its dispersion of agents yields a more diffuse and diverse composition of effective interventions. Electricity tends to favour complex ‘MBI + NMBI + T&G’ packages tailored to its capital-intensive, incumbent-dominated structure. Industry displays the mildest response, with cost sensitivity leading to a profile dominated by pricing and subsidies. In transport, the most effective interventions are dominated by ‘subsidy + targets’ combinations. This study suggests a general policy synergy pathway defined as ‘MBI as drivers + differentiated NMBI aligned with sectoral characteristics as complements + T&G as amplifiers’, which provides strong empirical evidence and practical guidance for designing LCT innovation policies. Nearly three-quarters of successful interventions combine multiple tools, and targets and governance should reinforce credibility rather than acting alone. Subsidies are the most consistent trigger of innovation and should anchor policy design, while performance standards are the most effective regulatory complement and merit wider coverage. Policy design should match each sector’s needs: diverse instruments for buildings, comprehensive packages for electricity, pricing and subsidies for industry, and subsidies with standards for transport. A generalizable synergy pathway, which is ‘market-based instruments as drivers, differentiated non-market-based instruments aligned with sectoral characteristics as complements, and target& governance as amplifiers’, provides a strategic blueprint for climate policy portfolio design.

title: Skills and Knowledge Exposure to the Twin Transition: A Multiregional, Multisectoral Analysis
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: The pace in which certain jobs with specific skills are demanded is changing rapidly. The so-called twin transition, comprising both digital and green transformations, is undoubtedly reshaping the economies, changing the way industries perf
content: The pace in which certain jobs with specific skills are demanded is changing rapidly. The so-called twin transition, comprising both digital and green transformations, is undoubtedly reshaping the economies, changing the way industries perform, and affecting the future of work across Europe. As the adoption of advanced digital technologies and low-carbon practices accelerate, the demand for new skills and knowledges increases, while other skills become outdated fast. The extent to which different countries, regions and sectors are exposed to these transformations is quite heterogeneous depending on their sectoral specialization and their capacity to adapt to these new technologies, creating disparities between the economies and polarization in the labour markets.This paper uses the OECD’s Intercountry Input-Output Tables for the year 2019 to analyse the exposure of the European countries, sectors, skills and knowledges to the twin transition. We extend the multiregional and multisectoral model, that accounts for trade spillovers between countries, with the information from European Commission’s ESCO (European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations) to provide labour demand by different categories. Additionally, to match both databases we use the European Labour Force Survey to connect the total employment by economic activity and occupations.Finally, by simulating the forecasted evolution of the different economic activities, we estimate shifts in labour market demands allowing us to identify the most vulnerable occupations, the number of jobs at risk in each country and sector, as well as the future demand for emerging skills. We believe that this type of analysis can provide valuable insights for policymakers and can serve as the basis for the design of tailored training programs.

title: Legume-based pathways reveal opportunities and limits of protein self-sufficiency in the EU and UK
summary: The European Union and United Kingdom (EU+) remain heavily dependent on imported high-protein feed, primarily soybeans, raising concerns about supply resilience and environmental impacts. We assess three legume-based pathways—trade, policy
content: The European Union and United Kingdom (EU+) remain heavily dependent on imported high-protein feed, primarily soybeans, raising concerns about supply resilience and environmental impacts. We assess three legume-based pathways—trade, policy support, and dietary shift—against a 2030 projection horizon, using integrated regional agro-economic, farm-level, and life cycle assessment models. The trade pathway, simulating a complete interruption of protein imports, provides an analytical upper bound for domestic EU+ legume production. It drives substantial land reallocation (+1.5 million ha legume area) but fails to fully replace imports, resulting in higher prices (+150% for soybeans) and reduced livestock output (-3%), exposing systemic vulnerabilities. Farm-level results underscore economic incentives over agroecological potential. Policy support moderately increases legume cultivation with limited market impacts but improves farm-level viability where conditions are favourable. Dietary shifts increase pulse imports (+100%) but reduce global GHG emissions more effectively than supply-side measures. Overall, the results highlight legumes’ potential, limits of self-sufficiency, and the complementary roles of economic incentives and demand-side measures for sustainable and resilient EU+ food systems. Assessing trade disruption, policy support, and dietary shifts shows that expanding legume production in the EU and UK improves resilience but cannot replace protein imports, while demand-side changes deliver greater climate benefits, based on integrated agro‑economic and life cycle modelling.

title: Profile Reconstruction via Deep Soil Mixing: A Practical Strategy for Mitigating Cadmium and Copper Availability in Naturally Enriched Vegetable Soils of Southwest China
summary: High natural heavy metal levels in Southwest China’s soils often lead to farmland contamination, and developing cost-effective risk mitigation strategies is crucial for safe agricultural production. This study evaluated profile reconstructi
content: High natural heavy metal levels in Southwest China’s soils often lead to farmland contamination, and developing cost-effective risk mitigation strategies is crucial for safe agricultural production. This study evaluated profile reconstruction of a copper (Cu)- and cadmium (Cd)-contaminated vegetable production base in Kunming via deep soil mixing. Soil profile analysis revealed a clear surface accumulation of Cd and available Cu/Cd in the topsoil. Deep plowing to a depth of 50 cm effectively reduced the available Cu and Cd concentrations in the newly formed topsoil from 5.60±1.81 mg kg⁻¹ to 2.09±1.77 mg kg⁻¹ (a 63% reduction) and from 0.143±0.064 mg kg⁻¹ to 0.032±0.035 mg kg⁻¹ (a 78% reduction), respectively. The intervention reduced the mean total Cd concentration to 0.22±0.11 mg kg⁻¹, alongside a drop in the Cd exceedance rate from 80% to 20%. Soil pH and phosphorus/potassium contents remained stable; however, levels of soil organic matter and available nitrogen declined significantly. Field experiments confirmed that deep plowing effectively reduced the Cu and Cd contents in the edible parts of vegetables. Therefore, deep tillage presents a practical and rapid strategy for mildly contaminated sites with vertical metal accumulation, allowing for simultaneous production and remediation.

title: Environmental vulnerability and governance in the Red River Delta, Vietnam: analysis and strategic recommendations
summary: Environmental vulnerability in deltaic regions is increasingly associated with governance failures rather than biophysical exposure alone. This study aims to examine how institutional arrangements shape household environmental vulnerability
content: Environmental vulnerability in deltaic regions is increasingly associated with governance failures rather than biophysical exposure alone. This study aims to examine how institutional arrangements shape household environmental vulnerability in Vietnam’s Red River Delta. An integrated mixed-methods approach was employed, combining household surveys (n = 1,000) across three provinces (Hanoi, Hung Yen, and Nam Dinh) using an adapted Household Vulnerability Assessment Tool (HVAT) with qualitative policy document analysis Results reveal that food security vulnerability (CVI2 = 0.245) is elevated across all income groups, while economic vulnerability concentrates among low-income households (CVI1 = 0.322). Psychosocial vulnerability ranks unexpectedly high overall (CVI5 = 0.185), particularly among high-income households (CVI5 = 0.220), while overall vulnerability is highest among low-income households (HVI = 0.210), followed by high-income (HVI = 0.181) and middle-income groups (HVI = 0.170), indicating that wealth alone does not eliminate environmental risks. Governance analysis identifies five institutional constraints associated with these vulnerabilities: subordination of environmental protection to economic development, procedural vagueness, exclusion of community participation, weak accountability, and implementation deficits. Each governance pattern corresponds to specific measured vulnerability outcomes, consistent with the proposition that institutional performance shapes environmental risk alongside biophysical exposure and economic resources. The recommendations indicate that effective vulnerability reduction in deltaic regions requires governance reforms prioritizing accountability mechanisms, community monitoring authority, and vulnerability-based policy frameworks rather than infrastructure investments alone.

title: How Circular Innovation Is Learned: A Process Study of Modularity‐Based Initiatives in Industrial Firms
summary: ABSTRACT Circular innovation (CI) research has identified a wide range of circular strategies and design approaches, yet offers limited insight into how CI evolves as a learning process within firms and which governance mechanisms guide thi
content: ABSTRACT Circular innovation (CI) research has identified a wide range of circular strategies and design approaches, yet offers limited insight into how CI evolves as a learning process within firms and which governance mechanisms guide this progression. Drawing on organizational learning (OL), this study examines how exploration and exploitation shape the CI process and how communication governs its progression. We study modularity, a prominent form of CI, through a 4‐year longitudinal qualitative study (2021–2025) based on 33 interviews across three Indian‐headquartered, globally operating firms in construction, electronics, and manufacturing. The study makes three contributions: (1) It contributes to the CI literature by theorizing CI as a learning process unfolding through three phases, learning the logic, learning to adapt and optimize, and learning to institutionalize, in which exploration and exploitation shift in salience and intensity as innovation progresses; (2) it extends CI research by conceptualizing communication as a governance mechanism that coordinates and stabilizes learning through feedback, cognitive, and social and behavioral control; and (3) it contributes to OL scholarship by showing that circular practices first generate operational memory, practical knowledge embedded in repair, recovery, and design routines, which communication gradually codifies into organizational memory that guides subsequent learning phases. Managerially, the study guides strategic leaders in governing CI through cross‐functional communication, operational managers in balancing experimentation with standardization and feedback routines, and firms in developing digital platforms that make learning visible across CI initiatives.

title: Equitable cooperation deepens the solution space for high ambition pathways
summary: Abstract Integrated assessment model scenarios informing global climate ambition typically treat fairness and cooperation as external to the modelling process, reinforcing a perceived tension between fair effort-sharing and the urgent colle
content: Abstract Integrated assessment model scenarios informing global climate ambition typically treat fairness and cooperation as external to the modelling process, reinforcing a perceived tension between fair effort-sharing and the urgent collective action needed to minimise exceedance of 1.5 °C. Here we introduce a generalisable framework that embeds principle-based fair-share considerations directly into the scenario generation process. This framework produces scenario variants that reconfigure transition pathways while preserving global peak and end of century climate outcomes. Exploring this space across allocation approaches, transfer limits, and cooperation mechanisms, we define a new lowest-feasible transfer scenario variant and examine the integrated system shifts it implies, contrasting it with the common exploration of fairness through ex-post assessments and unlimited financial transfers. We observe that the renewables deployment and electrification trajectories remain largely unchanged across all fair-share variants, while restricting transfers to lowest-feasible volumes accelerates global fossil decline, by up to 21% in 2040. This effect prevails even when interregional cooperation is focussed on financing carbon dioxide removal with geological storage, where higher-responsibility regions’ fair-share obligations remain met primarily through domestic gross emissions cuts. Against a globally cost-effective 2 °C (>67%) scenario that reduces consumption by approximately 0.8% relative to the no-new-policy baseline, we find that integrating fair-share transfers raises this to approximately 1.0% in total irrespective of approach and, where transfers are restricted to lowest-feasible volumes, to at most 1.5% in total. Notably, this aggregate is distributionally progressive, where lower-responsibility regions largely gain relative to the cost-effective source scenario. This deepened solution space persists even under a stringent 1.5 °C goal, though with differentiation increasingly settled through finance, and reveals dynamics that emerge only when scenario generation itself accounts for differentiated responsibilities and capabilities. Ultimately, we find that a ‘gross emissions reductions first’ strategy among higher-responsibility regions generates system-wide benefits, releasing pressure on lower-responsibility regions to collectively meet climate goals.
